History
The Wolfson History Prize has been awarded annually since 1972 by the Wolfson Foundation , an independent grant-making charity with a focus on research and education.
It was established largely on the initiative of the Wolfson Foundation’s then chairman, Leonard Wolfson, backed by trustees and other advisers, including the philosopher and historian Isaiah Berlin and the publisher George Weidenfeld.
…when we set up the prizes, the object was to encourage British historians to write in such a way that they would reach a general public and not barricade themselves behind their scholarly expertise to conduct a private debate.
Alan Bullock, former chair of judges and trustee of the Wolfson Foundation
The winners of the prize span the full range of historical enquiry: from biography to social, cultural and economic history to books about politics, war and international relations. All periods and geographic regions are represented. The roll call of winners – and the announcement of the prize each year – is a public statement of the importance of historical writing within British cultural life.

Timeline
50 years of the Wolfson History Prize
2022
The Wolfson History Prize celebrates its 50th anniversary
In its 50-year history, over £1.3 million has been awarded to 120 historians.
2021
Black Spartacus
The 2021 Wolfson History Prize is won by Sudhir Hazareesingh for ‘Black Spartacus: The Epic Life of Toussaint Louverture’, an account of the incredible life of the leader and hero of the Haitian Revolution.
2012
40th anniversary
For the prize’s 40th anniversary in 2012, Keith Thomas writes ‘An Informal History’. This draws on the Wolfson Foundation’s archive and his own memories.
Nikolaus Pevsner is the only winner to also have a biography about him win
Pevsner won in 1976 with his final book ‘A History of Building Types’, which marked the culmination of his career before his death in 1983. He became a household name for his colossal 46-volume series of county-by-county guides, ‘The Buildings of England’. Susie Harries’ biography, ‘Nikolaus Pevsner: The Life’, was based on exclusive access to his diaries and personal correspondence, as well as the professional archive for his guides.
2009
Mary Beard wins for Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town
In December 2010, Beard presented ‘Pompeii: Life and Death in a Roman Town’, taking viewers on a journey round the town as she had done for readers through her book. Her presenting career began after she was approached by former BBC Two controller Janice Hadlow, who had read her book about Pompeii while on holiday.
2000
History ‘on trial’
1989 winner and former judge, Richard Evans, is the main expert witness when David Irving sues the American academic Deborah Lipstadt after she accuses him of being a Holocaust denier in her book ‘Denying the Holocaust’. The trial made headlines all over the world and Evans was latterly portrayed by actors in TV documentaries, dramas and the 2017 feature film ‘Denial’. He wrote about his experience of the trial, and how he came to be involved, in the 2002 book ‘Telling Lies about Hitler’.
1998
Patricia Hollis wins for Jennie Lee: A Life
Hollis was a Labour peer who served as a welfare minister under Tony Blair. At the time she won the prize, she was a member of the House of Lords and a junior minister in the Department of Social Security.
1975
During International Women’s Year, both winners were women
The 1975 winners were Olwen Hufton for ‘The Poor of 18th-century France, 1750-1789’ and ‘Frances Donaldson (1907-1994) for ‘Edward VIII’. A farmer and writer, Donaldson’s first books were on farming before she turned to biography. After winning the Wolfson History Prize, Donaldson was an adviser on the BAFTA winning series ‘Edward and Mrs Simpson’, which brought a dramatised version of her book to television audiences in 1978. Image: Frances Annesley Donaldson (née Lonsdale), Lady Donaldson of Kingsbridge by Elliott & Fry © National Portrait Gallery, London.
1973
Veronica Wedgwood is appointed as judge, the first woman to hold the position
Wedgwood established herself as a historian with ‘The Thirty Years War’, published before she was 30. She was most well known to general audiences for her trilogy on the English Civil War, even though the final volume was never completed as planned. She received many honours recognising her work, including becoming the third woman (after Florence Nightingale and Dorothy Hodgkin) to be made a member of the Order of Merit, in 1969.
1972
First Wolfson Literary Awards for History presented
The first Wolfson Literary Awards for History, as they were known, were presented at a luncheon in the Dorchester Hotel and arose from an ambitious scheme proposed by Leonard Wolfson (1927-2010). Lord Wolfson originally envisioned multiple categories in various fields of scholarship and artistic achievement. These would be along the lines of the Nobel Prizes but avoiding any overlap in subject matter. Ultimately, the prize category was confined to ‘history’ in its widest sense.
